items.q: Type an expression for the number of ways to line up 5 different books on a shelf, and check its value.

mistakes.why: That counts only the first two places. All five places are filled: 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 5!.
Once a book is placed it cannot be used again, so the choices go down: 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.

options: That is $4^2$, not the factorial.
Right: $4! = 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$.
That is $4 + 3 + 2 + 1$; a factorial multiplies.
A factorial multiplies 4 by every whole number below it.

items.q: A quiz has 10 questions. Type an expression for the number of ways to choose which 3 questions a student gets right.

mistakes.why: That counts ordered choices. Which 3 questions are right does not depend on order, so divide by 3! = 6: 10C3.
Choosing 3 of 10 is not 10 × 3. Use the combination 10C3.

items.q: How many different teams of 2 can be chosen from 4 people?

why.correct: A team does not depend on order: ${}_4C_2 = \frac{4 \times 3}{2 \times 1} = 6$.
options: That counts ordered pairs: Ana then Ben is the same team as Ben then Ana, so divide by 2.
That is 4 × 2, which is not how choices combine.
That is $4^2$, which allows the same person twice and counts order.

items.q: Why does choosing 3 of 10 questions use a combination and not $10 \times 9 \times 8$?

why.correct: Ordered choices overcount each set by the number of its orders. Dividing by $3!$ gives the number of sets: $\frac{720}{6} = 120$.
options: Right: $10 \times 9 \times 8 = 720$ counts each set of 3 questions $3! = 6$ times, once for each order.
Calculators handle 720 easily; the problem is counting each set several times.
A combination chooses different items, with no repeats.
It counts ordered choices of 3, not the wrong answers.
The order in which the 3 questions are picked does not matter
$10 \times 9 \times 8$ is too large for a calculator
Combinations are used when questions can be repeated
$10 \times 9 \times 8$ counts the questions answered wrong
Choosing none is one way (the empty choice), so ${}_8C_0 = 1$.
There is just one way to take all 8 items.
Right: there is one way to choose none of the 8, and one way to choose all 8.
There is one way to choose nothing, not 8.

items.q: A pizza shop offers 6 toppings. How many different pizzas with exactly 3 different toppings are possible?

why.correct: Order does not matter and toppings do not repeat: ${}_6C_3 = 20$.
options: That counts ordered choices; the order of toppings on a pizza does not matter.
That is 6 × 3, which is not a count of choices.
That is $6^3$, which allows the same topping three times.
Right: ${}_6C_3 = \frac{6 \times 5 \times 4}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = 20$.
That is $12 \times 11$, an ordered count of two picks. Choosing 11 of 12 is the same as choosing the 1 to leave out.
Right: choosing 11 of the 12 is the same as choosing the 1 left out, and there are 12 ways to do that.
There are 12 different items that could be the one left out, not 11.

items.q: In which situation does the order matter, so that the count is a factorial and not a combination?

why.correct: A lineup counts orders, $4! = 24$. A choice of which items are in a group ignores order and uses a combination.
options: A committee is the same group whatever order its members were picked in: ${}_8C_3$.
The bag holds the same 2 fruits in either order: ${}_5C_2$.
Only which emails are flagged counts, not the order of flagging: ${}_{12}C_5$.
Right: a different left-to-right order is a different arrangement, so the count is $4! = 24$.
Choosing 3 of 8 students for a committee
Picking 2 of 5 fruits for a snack bag
Selecting which 5 of 12 emails to flag
Arranging 4 photos left to right on a wall

why.correct: ${}_8C_3 = \frac{8 \times 7 \times 6}{3!} = \frac{336}{6} = 56$. The $5!$ cancels, so only the top 3 factors are needed.

items.q: Ana (A), Ben (B) and Cal (C) form teams of 2. Which list shows every possible team exactly once?

why.correct: Order does not matter in a team, so there are ${}_3C_2 = 3$ teams: AB, AC and BC.
options: The team of Ana and Cal is missing.
BA is the same team as AB. This list counts each team twice, once in each order.
Right: ${}_3C_2 = \frac{3 \times 2}{2 \times 1} = 3$ teams, each listed once.
